name: Cesar Chavez
role: Labour leader and co-founder of the United Farm Workers (1927–1993)
summary: A farmworkers' union leader who co-founded the National Farm Workers Association and the United Farm Workers. He pursued change through nonviolent direct action such as boycotts, marches and fasts, grounded in Catholic social teaching and in Mexican-American and Chicano identity. He defended collective bargaining, attacked pesticide use and grower influence on politics, and changed his position on undocumented immigration over the 1970s.

unions-good.rationale: Calls the UFW 'first and foremost a union, a union like any other' and says it survives only by delivering bread-and-butter gains for members.

collective-bargaining.rationale: Says farm workers should be able to 'sit down and negotiate with your employer as equals across the bargaining table', and faults growers for refusing to bargain in good faith.

democracy-best.rationale: Describes the society he works within as 'a democratic society, where majority rules', and invokes the Bill of Rights in defending the union against charges of danger.

participatory-democracy.rationale: Stresses farm workers 'seizing control over their own lives' through votes, union elections and voter registration drives.

workplace-democracy.rationale: Pressed for free, secret-ballot union elections among workers, but the record does not show a position on how companies themselves are run.

worker-ownership.rationale: Reported by Wikipedia from biographers and his son: he saw workers' cooperatives as a middle path. Secondhand, so low.

neither-capitalism-nor-communism.rationale: Reported view, via Wikipedia's account of biographers, that cooperatives lay between a failed capitalism and state socialism.

dictatorship-of-proletariat.rationale: Inferred: he rejected Marxist-Leninist state socialism as a model in favour of cooperatives and nonviolence, per the Wikipedia account.

cooperative-communities.rationale: Promoted the La Paz commune, which held property in common, as a model others should follow. Reported by Wikipedia; does not extend to all of society.

correct-racial-injustice.rationale: Describes his union as attacking the 'historical source of shame and infamy' imposed on Mexican-Americans and speaks of racism and discrimination as wrongs to be overcome.

racism-not-main-obstacle.rationale: Inferred: his 1984 speech still describes ongoing discrimination in employment and in the fields, which points against saying racism has ceased to be the main obstacle.

racial-pride.rationale: Speaks of 'confidence and pride and hope' among Hispanics raised by the union, and of fighting for the dignity of his people.

racial-group-interests.rationale: Organised Mexican-American voters and workers as a community with shared interests, and Wikipedia reports he focused the movement on their ethnic identity.

individual-rights-only.rationale: Inferred: he organised as a community of farm workers and Mexican-Americans, which sits uneasily with holding that rights belong only to individuals.

intersecting-oppressions.rationale: Inferred: he links racial exclusion, class exploitation of farm labour and the sexual harassment of women workers within one struggle.

racial-segregation-law.rationale: Inferred: he describes being refused service in California because of his colour as an injustice, which implies opposition to laws separating races.

racial-franchise.rationale: Inferred: his voter-registration work for Mexican-Americans was a fight against exclusion from the franchise on racial grounds.

property-franchise.rationale: Inferred: his registration drives targeted poor and working people who did not own property, which implies opposition to a property test for voting.

equal-moral-worth.rationale: Says farm workers 'are not agricultural implements' and insists his people be treated 'as human beings and not as chattel'.

political-violence-never.rationale: His 1968 and 1972 fast statements call for nonviolence as the movement's only acceptable weapon, but he does not state an absolute rule for every case.

revolution-justified.rationale: Inferred: he rejected violence and pursued change through boycotts, fasts and elections rather than armed or revolutionary struggle.

direct-action.rationale: Wikipedia reports he judged boycotts and marches better than electoral politics, but after 1975 he redirected effort to elections under the state labour law.

means-match-ends.rationale: Inferred: his fasts and nonviolence were tied to the kind of society he wanted, a just and non-violent one.

war-builds-character.rationale: Inferred: Wikipedia reports he publicly opposed US involvement in the Vietnam War, but he makes no direct statement about war and character.

religion-illusion.rationale: Frames his movement as a Christian one and speaks of God as the giver of life, so he does not regard religion as mere consolation.

spiritual-nature.rationale: Fast statements speak of 'spirits', God and a spiritual commitment to justice alongside the material struggle over wages and conditions.

universal-morality.rationale: Inferred: his cause rests on Catholic social teaching, which holds moral principles to be universal, as Wikipedia describes.

reason-over-faith.rationale: Inferred: his movement drew its energy from faith and spiritual sacrifice as well as from organising reason.

more-religion-public.rationale: Inferred: he used Masses, processions and fasts in public campaigns and described the movement as a Christian radical philosophy.

self-interest-moral.rationale: Calls 'the greatest tragedy' a life without 'the satisfaction of giving life for others' and urges giving oneself totally to nonviolent struggle.

withdraw-from-politics.rationale: Spent his life in political organising, voter registration and campaigns, and says the movement's power comes from struggle in public life.

animal-suffering-matters.rationale: Wikipedia reports he became a vegetarian in 1970 and said cows and dogs are 'about the same', a secondhand quote.

animal-use-humane.rationale: Inferred: he became a vegetarian in 1970 and rejected meat-eating, which points against using animals for food even humanely.

precautionary-principle.rationale: In the 1986 Wrath of Grapes speech he says no one can define safe exposure to residual poison, so consumers must be warned and act now.

gm-crops.rationale: Criticises produce that results from 'plant mutations or chemicals' and says food should be free of toxics; a judgement on engineered crops is not stated.

nature-intrinsic-value.rationale: Describes damage to the land as a 'wanton abuse of nature', which treats nature as worth protecting for its own sake, though he does not state this directly.

future-generations.rationale: Pleads for protection from poisons for 'our children and for their children', a concern for future generations that is not framed as stewardship of the Earth.

patriotism-serves-workers.rationale: Calls the boycott 'a fight for the future of America' and speaks of 'one family', linking national interest with the welfare of workers.

material-over-identity.rationale: Inferred: the movement built its identity around Mexican-American and Chicano ethnicity as well as material demands, per Wikipedia.

profit-exploitation.rationale: Accuses growers of abusing and exploiting the workers who produce their wealth; he does not state a general theory of profit.

regulate-corporations.rationale: Calls for enforcing the law against growers who break it and for protecting consumers from pesticide residues; a broader position on corporate regulation is not stated.

reduce-immigration.rationale: Contested. His 1974 letter favours liberalised immigration law and amnesty and opposes deportation, while the Illegals Campaign and the wet line aimed to remove undocumented strikebreakers. The evidence points both ways.

suppress-opposition.rationale: No stated position on suppressing political opposition; expelling dissenters inside his own union is something nearby.

notes: Positions were checked against his own words where available: the 1984 Commonwealth Club address (full transcript), the 1986 Wrath of Grapes excerpt, and his 1968 and 1972 fast statements. The Wrath of Grapes text is a seven-minute excerpt, not the full speech. The Foundation's archive and the 1968 nonviolence and 1975 farm labor law texts were unreachable, so the 1975 act is only covered through his 1984 speech. His immigration stance is the most contested part of the record. The 1974 letter (quoted via s5) is the most recent clear statement found on immigration, and the Illegals Campaign and wet line (both 1973–1974, reported in s4) point the other way, so the answer is 0 at low confidence. His Vietnam opposition and vegetarianism come from Wikipedia and are secondhand. No position was found on the great majority of statements, so most are null.
